  • Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning (SCoRe): the training-time successor to the arc, moving the external correctness signal from inference-time scaffolding into RL reward.
  • Truly Self-Improving Agents Require Intrinsic Metacognitive Learning: a framework for why a model deciding what to learn differs from running a designer-fixed self-correction loop.
  • AbstRaL: Augmenting LLMs’ Reasoning by Reinforcing Abstract Thinking: another reinforcement-learning route to more reliable reasoning, complementary to gating revision on an external signal.

item.title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning [1] (NeurIPS 2023), Noah Shinn et al. (Northeastern, MIT, Princeton) introduce an agent architecture that “learns” across episodes purely by writing natural-language reflections to an episodic memory, without gradient updates or weight changes.

Large language models (LLMs) have been increasingly used to interact with external environments (e.g., games, compilers, APIs) as goal-driven agents. However, it remains challenging for these language agents to quickly and efficiently learn from trial-and-error as traditional reinforcement learning methods require extensive training samples and expensive model fine-tuning. We propose Reflexion, a novel framework to reinforce language agents not by updating weights, but instead through linguistic feedback. Concretely, Reflexion agents verbally reflect on task feedback signals, then maintain their own reflective text in an episodic memory buffer to induce better decision-making in subsequent trials. Reflexion is flexible enough to incorporate various types (scalar values or free-form language) and sources (external or internally simulated) of feedback signals, and obtains significant improvements over a baseline agent across diverse tasks (sequential decision-making, coding, language reasoning). For example, Reflexion achieves a 91% pass@1 accuracy on the HumanEval coding benchmark, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art GPT-4 that achieves 80%.

Methods

The agent operates by interaction: at each step it emits an action — a tool call, environment command, or free-form answer — and the environment returns an observation. A single attempt at the task is an episode (also called a trial), and the action-observation sequence within one episode is the trajectory () — the agent’s short-term memory.

The Reflexion framework factors the agent into three roles. The Self-Reflection model is always an LLM. The Actor is always an LLM, and in most setups the same LLM as the Self-Reflection model, with different prompts. The Evaluator can be an LLM but is often a non-LLM signal: a hand-written heuristic, exact-match grading, or the pass/fail of a generated test suite.

  • Actor () — an LLM whose weights, together with the current experience buffer, jointly parameterize the policy from which each next action is sampled ().
  • Evaluator () — scores the resulting trajectory: a hand-written heuristic (or an LLM-as-judge variant) on AlfWorld, the pass/fail of self-generated unit tests on HumanEval, exact-match grading on HotPotQA’s final answer.
  • Self-Reflection () — takes the trajectory plus the evaluator’s signal and produces a short natural-language reflection (e.g. “I failed because I assumed they both had the same professions”), appended to the experience buffer — the agent’s long-term memory that persists across episodes.

On the next episode, the Actor is conditioned on the accumulated experience and attempts the task again. The LLM weights stay fixed; the only thing that updates between episodes is the experience text. The “reinforcement signal” is literally the reflection text the Self-Reflection model writes after each failure.

Results

The paper evaluates Reflexion on three task families:

  • AlfWorld [2] (sequential decision-making, 134 task instances) — Reflexion adds 22 percentage points absolute over a ReAct [3] baseline within 12 iterative learning steps, and the best variant solves 130 of 134 tasks. Figure 3(a) tracks cumulative tasks solved by trial number under both self-evaluation modes (a hand-written heuristic and a GPT-as-judge classifier); 3(b) decomposes the residual failures into hallucination and inefficient planning — both decay steadily under Reflexion, while the ReAct-only baseline plateaus.
  • HotPotQA [4] (multi-hop reasoning) — Reflexion improves accuracy by 20 points on a 100-question subset. Figure 4 separates the contribution: (a) Reflexion benefits both ReAct and Chain-of-Thought actors; (b) the gain holds even when the actor is given the ground-truth context, so it isn’t just better retrieval; (c) decomposes the lift between including past trajectories (episodic memory) and the verbal Self-Reflection step. Episodic memory accounts for most of the gain, and Self-Reflection adds an 8-point boost on top.
  • HumanEval [5] (Python coding, GPT-4 as Actor) — Reflexion reaches 91% pass@1 versus the reported 80% GPT-4 baseline (11-point gain). Table 1 shows the gain is consistent across languages and benchmarks: HumanEval Rust 60 → 68, MBPP [6] (Mostly Basic Programming Problems) Rust 71 → 75. The paper also introduces LeetcodeHardGym, a benchmark of 40 hard-rated Leetcode problems with scaffolding across 19 programming languages, but only reports results on the Python subset (7.5 → 15); the multi-language scope is released as an artifact, not used in any reported experiment. The exception to the across-the-board gains is MBPP Python, where Reflexion (77.1) underperforms the GPT-4 baseline (80.1) — see the test-generation table below.

The paper’s ablations compare self-generated unit tests vs ground-truth tests as the evaluation signal, examine memory-length effects, and separate the contribution of the Evaluator from the Self-Reflection step. Two things to flag about Table 2 before reading. First, the test suites used as the Evaluator’s signal are all LLM-generated: Reflexion’s procedure is the same on every code benchmark — the Actor writes tests from the problem description (with chain-of-thought prompting), filters for syntactic validity, and uses those tests’ pass/fail as the signal. MBPP ships with its own curated tests, but Reflexion doesn’t use them; the model generates fresh tests from the prompt. Second, the four diagnostic columns are conditional probabilities: TP and FP are conditional on tests passing (TP + FP = 1), FN and TN on tests failing (FN + TN = 1).

The Base and Reflexion columns are pass@1 — the approach’s headline accuracy with and without the Reflexion loop. The TP / FN / FP / TN columns rate the LLM-generated tests as a classifier of solution correctness, and they predict approach performance directly. HumanEval Python’s tests are clean — TP=0.99, FP=0.01 — and Reflexion lifts 0.80 → 0.91. MBPP Python’s tests are noisy on both sides: FP=0.16 lets buggy code through, FN=0.59 means most “test failures” were actually correct solutions the loop then rewrites, and Reflexion drops to 0.77.

The paper doesn’t diagnose why MBPP’s LLM-generated tests are noisier, but the prompt structure of the two benchmarks is a plausible explanation: HumanEval prompts are docstrings that often include doctest-style I/O examples (the LLM can crib from those when writing tests), while MBPP prompts are bare natural-language sentences (“Write a function to remove duplicates…”) with no I/O examples, so the LLM has to invent both inputs and expected outputs from scratch.

My Notes

  • Verbal feedback as policy state. Reflexion is the paper that established natural-language reflection as a first-class component of agent design, and the lineage is visible across 2024 agentic frameworks — from AutoGen [7] to LangGraph to the critic-refiner loops in Anthropic’s computer-use agents. What’s distinctive here is keeping the reflections as long-term memory across trials rather than compressing them into the immediate context the way Self-Refine [8] does.
  • The 91% HumanEval caveat. Later reproductions found Reflexion’s gain is bottlenecked by test-generation quality rather than by the repair step itself: Olausson et al. (2024) [9] studied iterative self-repair on HumanEval and APPS and argued that “self-repair is bottlenecked by the model’s ability to provide feedback on its own code” — substituting a stronger feedback model lifts the gains substantially. Reflexion’s own ablation (Table 3 on HumanEval Rust) tells the same story: removing test generation drops Reflexion from 0.68 to 0.52, while removing the self-reflection step alone barely moves the number (0.68 → 0.60). CodeT [10] makes the self-generated-test mechanism explicit; Reflexion adds a reflection step on top but inherits CodeT’s dependence on test-generation quality.
  • Reflexion vs Cannot-Self-Correct. Reflexion’s headline claim — that verbal reinforcement lifts an LLM agent — runs alongside a result by Huang et al. [11] that LLMs cannot reliably self-correct. The two don’t contradict.
    • Huang et al. define intrinsic self-correction as a model revising its own answer with no external signal, and show it degrades reasoning. Reflexion always supplies an external signal via the Evaluator — a heuristic on AlfWorld, exact-match on HotPotQA, test execution on HumanEval.
    • The structural overlap is Reflexion’s Self-Reflection step. Diagnosing what went wrong over the model’s own trajectory is exactly what Huang et al. studied. The Evaluator is upstream: it gates whether Self-Reflection fires at all.
    • Table 2 backs this up with the FN column: MBPP Python’s FN is 0.59 vs HumanEval Python’s 0.40, meaning MBPP’s tests fail on already-correct solutions much more often. Reflexion then “corrects” those correct solutions and ends up below the GPT-4 baseline on MBPP Python — 80.1 (baseline) vs 77.1 (Reflexion).
    • So Reflexion is best read as a positive existence result for self-correction with reliable external signal, not a refutation of the intrinsic-failure result.
  • Memory-as-parameters has a context budget. The paper writes the policy as with — the memory is part of the parameter set. The interesting question is what learning in token space gives up. First, the experience is task-specific and doesn’t transfer: every new task starts with an empty buffer. Second, as the buffer grows across trials, the Actor’s context budget becomes the bottleneck, so the effective “learning rate” is bounded by how much context the system can spend per inference. Later work on extending effective context (MemGPT [12]) and agent-specific long-context finetuning is partly a response to this limit.

item.title: Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet [1] (ICLR 2024), Jie Huang, Xinyun Chen, Swaroop Mishra, Huaixiu Steven Zheng, Adams Wei Yu, Xinying Song, and Denny Zhou (Google DeepMind + UIUC) argue that intrinsic self-correction — where a model revises its own reasoning answer with no external signal about correctness — does not improve and often degrades performance on reasoning benchmarks.

Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a groundbreaking technology with their unparalleled text generation capabilities across various applications. Nevertheless, concerns persist regarding the accuracy and appropriateness of their generated content. A contemporary methodology, self-correction, has been proposed as a remedy to these issues. Building upon this premise, this paper critically examines the role and efficacy of self-correction within LLMs, shedding light on its true potential and limitations. Central to our investigation is the notion of intrinsic self-correction, whereby an LLM attempts to correct its initial responses based solely on its inherent capabilities, without the crutch of external feedback. In the context of reasoning, our research indicates that LLMs struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback, and at times, their performance even degrades after self-correction. Drawing from these insights, we offer suggestions for future research and practical applications in this field.

Methods

The paper isolates intrinsic self-correction by stripping out the external verifier that prior self-correction work relied on. In the oracle setting (used by RCI [2] and Reflexion [3] in their reported evaluations), the loop has access to the gold-label answer:

  1. Model generates an answer.
  2. Compare it to the ground truth (the oracle).
  3. If correct, stop. If wrong, prompt the model for a critique, generate a revision, return to step 2.

The oracle is doing two jobs at once: it’s a stopping condition (don’t keep revising correct answers) and a trigger for revision (only revise when wrong). In the intrinsic setting, both jobs go away. The same model produces the initial answer, then is prompted to review and revise it without any external check, and has to decide on its own whether the answer needs further work. The evaluation runs on three reasoning datasets — GSM8K [10] (grade-school math), CommonSenseQA [11] (multiple-choice commonsense), and HotpotQA [12] (multi-hop QA) — across GPT-3.5-Turbo (gpt-3.5-turbo-0613), GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo (gpt-4-1106-preview), and Llama-2-70b-chat [4]. Each round of self-correction costs two additional model calls (review, then revision), so two rounds bring the total per question to five.

The paper then re-examines two related claims from prior work:

  • Section 4 revisits multi-agent debate [5], where several LLM agents propose answers and critique each other across rounds until they converge on a consensus. The paper reproduces Du et al. [5]’s setup on GSM8K and compares it against self-consistency [6] — generating multiple independent samples and majority-voting — at the same total response budget.
  • Section 5 revisits Self-Refine [7], where the same LLM generates an output, critiques it, and refines based on its own critique over multiple iterations. The paper attributes Self-Refine’s reported gains on constrained generation to a sub-optimal initial prompt that the refinement loop is largely just patching.

Results

  • Intrinsic self-correction degrades accuracy across every model tested. With oracle labels (Table 2 of the paper), self-correction improves modestly — GPT-3.5 on GSM8K rises from 75.9 to 84.3, GPT-4 on HotpotQA from 49.0 to 59.0. Without oracle labels, the same prompts and models lose accuracy. After two rounds of intrinsic self-correction, GPT-3.5 on GSM8K drops from 75.9 to 74.7. On CommonSenseQA the drop is sharper, 75.8 to 41.8. GPT-4 holds up better but still loses 6.5 points on GSM8K (95.5 → 89.0). Llama-2-70b-chat collapses, halving from 62.0 to 36.5 on GSM8K. The cover image’s Figure 1 decomposition shows why: correct → incorrect transitions outnumber incorrect → correct ones, so the loop is on average destructive.
  • Multi-agent debate underperforms self-consistency at matched budget. With three agents over two rounds of debate, the system uses nine total responses and reaches 83.0 on GSM8K. Self-consistency with nine responses reaches 88.2 with the same model. At every matched budget, simple majority voting beats the debate protocol. The paper concludes that what looks like critique is in practice a noisier form of consensus.

My Notes

  • The RL follow-up. Two follow-ups from this same group at Google DeepMind reframe the negative result rather than overturn it. SCoRe [8] trains Gemini 1.0 Pro and 1.5 Flash via multi-turn RL to actually self-correct on MATH, gaining 15.6 points on top of the base model — explicitly citing this paper as the problem statement. The o1-style training paradigm builds correction into the chain-of-thought RL signal itself. The conclusion of Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet is essentially that prompting alone cannot induce self-correction in models that were not trained for it; the field has since shown that the right RL objective can.
  • The oracle-label confound is the methodological core. The paper’s most reusable contribution is naming the evaluation issue: RCI [2] and Reflexion [3] let the loop terminate based on whether the answer was correct, which leaks ground truth into the evaluation. Once you remove that signal, the loop runs without a stop condition and tends to drift. This generalizes: any test-time loop that uses the gold answer to decide when to halt is implicitly conditioning on it. The same issue surfaces in process reward model evaluation, where a strong external verifier provides most of the signal that gets attributed to the generator.
  • Production loops have implicit signals. Real systems usually carry external signals that the paper’s “no oracle” definition excludes: format checks, runnable code, type errors, schema violations, factual lookups against retrieval. Reflexion [3], for instance, uses an environment reward (test pass/fail, task success). The paper’s negative result is for the strict version where the model has nothing to go on but its own prior; that is the version closest to “talking to yourself,” which is also the version least likely to converge.
  • Multi-agent debate as ensembling. Section 4’s finding that multi-agent debate underperforms self-consistency at matched response budget [5][6] has been replicated repeatedly since, across the multi-agent literature, including the MAST taxonomy of multi-agent failure modes [9]. Stripped of training, much of what looks like agent collaboration reduces to weighted voting on independent samples, where the sampling budget determines the result rather than the protocol.

item.title: Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback [1] (NeurIPS 2023), Aman Madaan, Niket Tandon, and collaborators at CMU, Allen Institute for AI, University of Washington, NVIDIA, UC San Diego, and Google Research show that a single frozen large language model (LLM) can act as generator, critic, and rewriter in a prompt-only loop, and that this loop improves outputs across seven generation tasks without any additional training.

Like humans, large language models (LLMs) do not always generate the best output on their first try. Motivated by how humans refine their written text, we introduce Self-Refine, an approach for improving initial outputs from LLMs through iterative feedback and refinement. The main idea is to generate an initial output using an LLMs; then, the same LLMs provides feedback for its output and uses it to refine itself, iteratively. Self-Refine does not require any supervised training data, additional training, or reinforcement learning, and instead uses a single LLM as the generator, refiner, and feedback provider. We evaluate Self-Refine across 7 diverse tasks, ranging from dialog response generation to mathematical reasoning, using state-of-the-art (GPT-3.5, ChatGPT, and GPT-4) LLMs. Across all evaluated tasks, outputs generated with Self-Refine are preferred by humans and automatic metrics over those generated with the same LLM using conventional one-step generation, improving by ~20% absolute on average in task performance. Our work demonstrates that even state-of-the-art LLMs like GPT-4 can be further improved at test time using our simple, standalone approach.

Methods

The method is deliberately minimal. Self-Refine takes an input , uses three handcrafted few-shot prompts — p_gen, p_fb, p_refine — and runs the same model three ways: produces the initial output ; emits natural-language feedback on ; and the refine step writes from the model conditioned on the input plus the full history of prior outputs and feedback (). No fine-tuning, no external reward model, no reinforcement learning. The loop halts either at a fixed iteration budget or when itself signals that no further refinement is needed. The paper evaluates on dialogue response generation, code optimization, code readability improvement, mathematical reasoning (GSM8K [5]), sentiment reversal, acronym generation, and constrained generation, with base models GPT-3.5 (text-davinci-003 and gpt-3.5-turbo), ChatGPT, Codex [6] (code-davinci-002), and GPT-4.

Two things distinguish the prompts from generic “what do you think?” critique prompting. First, p_fb is few-shot-exemplified to elicit feedback that is actionable (names a concrete change to make) and specific (pinpoints the exact phrase or line to change). The Figure 2(e) example — “This code is slow as it uses a for loop… A better approach is to use the formula (n(n+1))/2” — is the template: identify the offending construct, propose the replacement. Second, p_refine is also few-shot, with quadruples that show how to translate feedback into a concrete edit rather than paraphrase or hedge.

The few-shot exemplars in p_fb are themselves built from a per-task rubric — 10 qualitative aspects for Dialogue Response Generation (relevant, informative, interesting, consistent, etc.), a 5-dimension rubric for Acronym Generation (pronunciation, spelling, etc.), the missing-concept checklist for Constrained Generation. The rubric is never invoked explicitly at inference. The model learns it from the exemplars.

Results

Across the seven tasks, Self-Refine beats single-shot prompting by 5–40 points absolute, averaging around 20 points of improvement by human preference and automatic metrics. The gains are largest on tasks with multifaceted or hard-to-define objectives (dialogue, code readability, constrained generation) and smallest on math reasoning, where Table 1 shows essentially no improvement (↑0 to ↑0.2) — the paper attributes this to the feedback model’s inability to detect subtle math errors. Code optimization improves by 8.7 points absolute on GPT-4 (27.3 → 36.0), and by up to 13 points absolute when applied to Codex. Human raters prefer Self-Refine outputs at rates generally consistent with the automatic metrics. The paper releases prompts and code.

The paper also ablates the feedback prompt itself, replacing actionable+specific feedback with generic “what do you think?” feedback or no feedback at all (Table 2). The actionable+specific shape carries most of the signal, especially on tasks where “good output” is hard to define — Sentiment Reversal goes from 43.2 to 31.2 to 0 across the three feedback regimes. On Code Optimization, where “fast” is well-defined, generic feedback already gets you most of the way there.

My Notes

  • The gain doesn’t generalize beyond strong critics. The ~20-point headline held up in the paper’s own benchmarks but is sensitive to task and model. Kamoi et al. [4]’s survey concludes that no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback generated by LLMs prompting themselves under fair settings, and they specifically flag Self-Refine’s evaluation as over-stating the gain (Table 4 of the survey: weak prompts on the initial-response side combined with appropriate prompts on the self-correction side). On reasoning tasks, Huang et al. [2] show intrinsic self-correction can degrade accuracy on average — Table 1’s near-zero math result here was already a tell. The loop assumes the critic produces actionable feedback. When the critic is weak (smaller models make this worse rather than introduce it), the iterations don’t help.
  • Feedback quality drives more gain than iteration count. The paper omits the cleanest ablation: a single-pass critique-and-refine prompt that gives the base LLM the rubric without iteration. Without it, a substantial part of the gain on dialogue and constrained generation may be attributable to the rubric embedded in the feedback prompt rather than to iteration itself. Reflexion [3], which appeared around the same time, makes the memory question explicit: it persists verbal reflections across episodes, while Self-Refine’s history is scoped to a single input.
  • The prompt-only antecedent of o1. Self-Refine spends several times more tokens per problem than one-shot generation in exchange for task-quality gains — the same compute-for-quality tradeoff that o1-style models would later formalize with RL-trained chains, but realized through prompting alone. In 2023 the framing was novel. The test-time compute idiom only entered general usage with the o1 release in late 2024.

item.title: Promptbreeder: Self-Referential Self-Improvement Via Prompt Evolution
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Promptbreeder: Self-Referential Self-Improvement Via Prompt Evolution [1], Fernando et al. at Google DeepMind propose an evolutionary prompt optimizer in which the large language model (LLM) mutates both the task prompts it evaluates and the mutation prompts that generate them, yielding a self-referential loop without any gradient updates.

Popular prompt strategies like Chain-of-Thought Prompting can dramatically improve the reasoning abilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) in various domains. However, such hand-crafted prompt-strategies are often sub-optimal. In this paper, we present Promptbreeder, a general-purpose self-referential self-improvement mechanism that evolves and adapts prompts for a given domain. Driven by an LLM, Promptbreeder mutates a population of task-prompts, and subsequently evaluates them for fitness on a training set. Crucially, the mutation of these task-prompts is governed by mutation-prompts that the LLM generates and improves throughout evolution in a self-referential way. That is, Promptbreeder is not just improving task-prompts, but it is also improving the mutation-prompts that improve these task-prompts. Promptbreeder outperforms state-of-the-art prompt strategies such as Chain-of-Thought and Plan-and-Solve Prompting on commonly used arithmetic and commonsense reasoning benchmarks. Furthermore, Promptbreeder is able to evolve intricate task-prompts for the challenging problem of hate speech classification.

Methods

Promptbreeder maintains a population of “units of evolution,” each consisting of two sequentially applied task prompts and one mutation prompt. A binary tournament genetic algorithm picks two units, scores both on a training minibatch, and replaces the loser with a mutated copy of the winner. The initial population is seeded from a library of 39 generic “thinking-style” hints (Appendix D of the paper), combined with an LLM-written problem description. The 39 hints fall into four flavors:

  • Concrete strategies — “Let’s think step by step.” (#38), “Let’s make a step by step plan and implement it with good notion and explanation.” (#39), “How can I break down this problem into smaller, more manageable parts?” (#9), “How could I devise an experiment to help solve that problem?” (#1).
  • Cognitive-style labels — “Critical Thinking: …” (#10), “Try creative thinking, generate innovative and out-of-the-box ideas…” (#11), “Use systems thinking: …” (#13), “Use Reflective Thinking: …” (#15).
  • Diagnostic questions — “What is the core issue or problem that needs to be addressed?” (#16), “What are the key assumptions underlying this problem?” (#5), “Are there any stakeholders or individuals who are directly affected by the problem?” (#21).
  • Reframings — “Given the problem specification and the current best solution, have a guess about other possible solutions.” (#34), “Let’s imagine the current best solution is totally wrong, what other ways are there to think about the problem specification?” (#35), “Ignoring the current best solution, create an entirely new solution to the problem.” (#37).

The search uses PaLM 2-L as both proposer and executor.

Nine mutation operators across five classes drive the search:

  • Direct mutation — the LLM rewrites the task prompt directly.
  • Estimation-of-distribution mutation — generate new prompts conditioned on a sample of high-fitness prompts from the population, summarizing what’s working.
  • Hyper-mutation — zero-shot and few-shot variants that use the unit’s current mutation prompt to drive the rewrite.
  • Lamarckian mutation — infer a new task prompt from correctly solved examples (the trace becomes the genotype).
  • Crossover and mutation-prompt mutation — recombine units, and separately evolve the mutation prompts themselves so the search strategy itself adapts over generations.

The four panels in Figure 2 trace the conceptual escalation: (a) direct rewriting, (b) mutation-prompt guidance, (c) hyper-mutation that evolves the mutation prompt itself, and (d) the full Promptbreeder population over thinking-styles, mutation-prompts, and the problem description. Solid arrows are inputs into the LLM in one forward pass. Dashed arrows are the cross-generational flows: each output (P′, M′) becomes the parent for the next round, and in panel (d) the mutation prompt M is sampled from the evolving population ℳ rather than being hand-written.

Results

The paper evaluates Promptbreeder on arithmetic reasoning (GSM8K, SVAMP, MultiArith, AQuA-RAT, AddSub, SingleEq), commonsense reasoning (CommonsenseQA, StrategyQA), and hate-speech classification on ETHOS [2]. Promptbreeder uses PaLM 2-L; older Chain-of-Thought, Plan-and-Solve, and Program-of-Thoughts baselines run on text-davinci-003, while APE [3] and OPRO [4] are reimplemented under PaLM 2-L for the matched comparison. Asterisked datasets (MultiArith*, SingleEq*, AddSub*, SVAMP*) used half the examples for training and report accuracy on the held-out half; bracketed numbers in the table are quoted directly from the Plan-and-Solve paper’s text-davinci-003 results.

Headline findings (PB row leads every column of both zero-shot and few-shot categories):

  • Arithmetic reasoning — 99.7% on MultiArith*, 96.4% on SingleEq*, 90.2% on SVAMP*, 87.8% on AddSub*, 83.9% on GSM8K, 62.2% on AQuA-RAT (zero-shot).
  • Commonsense reasoning — 71.8% on StrategyQA, 80.2% on CommonsenseQA (zero-shot).
  • Beats prior prompt optimizers under matched PaLM 2-L: above APE and OPRO [4] on every dataset where both report a number.

The paper’s ablation (Figure 4) removes one self-referential operator at a time and reports the percentage change in fitness vs the full algorithm. Each ablation mode:

  • Hyper — remove mutation-prompt mutation (the “self-referential” core feature).
  • Lamarck — remove the Context-to-task-prompt mutation (Lamarckian operator: infer the task prompt from correctly solved examples).
  • SR task-prompt — remove thinking-style-guided task-prompt initialization (the seed library).
  • SR mut-prompt — remove random selection of a mutation prompt from the mutation-prompt list.

Negative cells mean removing that operator drops fitness — the operator helps. Positive cells mean removing it raises fitness — the operator is actively hurting on that dataset.

The picture is uneven. SR task-prompt (thinking-style seeding) shows the largest negative value on 6 of 8 datasets: −80% on StrategyQA, −74% on SVAMP, −73% on GSM8K, and by far the largest average drop (≈ −58%, vs ≈ −30% for Hyper and Lamarck), making it the single most important operator. SR mut-prompt is the noisiest: it’s mildly helpful on most rows but actively hurts GSM8K (+41%) and is near zero on AQUA_DEV (+1%) and MultiArith (+9%), so the random-mutation-prompt-selection mechanism isn’t carrying weight uniformly. Hyper and Lamarck are roughly comparable in magnitude, with neither consistently dominating across datasets.

My Notes

  • Self-referential framing oversold. Having the LLM mutate the prompts that mutate its task prompts hints at Schmidhuber’s self-referential weight matrix work [5] from the 1990s, but in practice the second-order mutation-prompt mutation is a further LLM call with a fixed meta-prompt. The paper’s own ablation (Figure 4) shows mutation-prompt mutation (Hyper) is roughly on par with the Lamarckian operator on average and is dwarfed by the impact of thinking-style seeding (SR task-prompt). The “self-referential” framing matters less than the title implies.
  • From operator menus to feedback signals. Promptbreeder lists nine mutation operators across five classes, and much of the win over APE [3] and Chain-of-Thought comes from this richer toolkit of edits rather than from the tournament selection itself. Since 2023, prompt-optimization research has shifted from genetic-algorithm operators toward gradient-free Bayesian surrogates (MIPROv2 [7]) and reflective critique driven by trajectory-level natural-language feedback (GEPA [6], TextGrad [8] ). The field has moved toward richer feedback signals rather than richer operator menus.
  • Thinking-style seeding is the biggest contributor. The initial population is seeded by combining the problem description with a library of generic reasoning hints (“let’s think step by step,” “let’s work backwards from the answer”) listed in Appendix D. The paper treats this as a minor detail, but Figure 4 shows that removing the thinking-style seeding (SR task-prompt) has the largest negative impact on 6 of 8 datasets, with an average fitness drop roughly twice that of removing mutation-prompt mutation or the Lamarckian operator. Much of what Promptbreeder “evolves” is downstream of a good seed.

  2. Mollas, I., Chrysopoulou, Z., Karlos, S., Tsoumakas, G. “ETHOS: an Online Hate Speech Detection Dataset.” Complex & Intelligent Systems, arXiv:2006.08328, June 11, 2020. https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.08328

item.title: Large Language Models Are Human-Level Prompt Engineers (APE)
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Large Language Models Are Human-Level Prompt Engineers [1] (ICLR 2023), Zhou et al. (University of Toronto, Vector Institute, University of Waterloo) propose Automatic Prompt Engineer (APE), a black-box search that uses one large language model (LLM) to write candidate natural-language instructions for a task, then selects the best via the zero-shot performance of a second LLM.

By conditioning on natural language instructions, large language models (LLMs) have displayed impressive capabilities as general-purpose computers. However, task performance depends significantly on the quality of the prompt used to steer the model, and most effective prompts have been handcrafted by humans. Inspired by classical program synthesis and the human approach to prompt engineering, we propose Automatic Prompt Engineer (APE) for automatic instruction generation and selection. In our method, we treat the instruction as the “program,” optimized by searching over a pool of instruction candidates proposed by an LLM in order to maximize a chosen score function. To evaluate the quality of the selected instruction, we evaluate the zero-shot performance of another LLM following the selected instruction. Extensive experiments show that our automatically generated instructions outperform the prior LLM baseline by a large margin and achieve better or comparable performance to the instructions generated by human annotators on 24/24 Instruction Induction tasks and 17/21 curated BIG-Bench tasks. We conduct extensive qualitative and quantitative analyses to explore the performance of APE. We show that APE-engineered prompts are able to improve few-shot learning performance (by simply prepending them to standard in-context learning prompts), find better zero-shot chain-of-thought prompts, as well as steer models toward truthfulness and/or informativeness.

Methods

APE casts instruction design as a program-synthesis problem over natural-language programs. Given a small set of input-output demonstrations:

  1. Propose. A proposer LLM generates candidate instructions in one of two ways:
    • Forward generation — “here are examples, write the instruction.”
    • Reverse infilling — the proposer fills in an <INSERT> slot placed between inputs and outputs.
    Forward mode is the default and works on any pretrained LLM, but constrains the instruction to sit at the end of the prompt. Reverse mode requires a proposer with infilling capability (e.g., T5, GLM, InsertGPT, or InstructGPT’s <INSERT> token) and lets the instruction be placed mid-prompt, which the authors find more flexible. The paper uses forward mode for the Instruction Induction experiments and reverse mode for BIG-Bench. The choice is the user’s, not an algorithmic gate inside APE.
  2. Score. Each candidate is run through an executor LLM on a held-out set; the score is task accuracy or log-probability of the correct output.
  3. (Optional) resample. Monte Carlo resampling asks the proposer to generate semantically similar variants of the best candidates and re-scores them.
  4. Select. The instruction with the highest score wins.

No fine-tuning is involved and the method treats both the proposer and the executor as black boxes.

Results

The paper evaluates APE on the 24 NLP tasks from the Instruction Induction [2] benchmark [2], plus the BIG-Bench Instruction Induction subset and TruthfulQA [3]. It compares three sources of instructions:

  • APE — the full propose-score-select pipeline.
  • Greedy — Honovich et al.’s [2] prior algorithm, which takes the proposer’s first sample without any selection step.
  • Human — gold annotations written by the original Instruction Induction annotators.

With InstructGPT (175B) as both proposer and executor, APE reaches an interquartile mean of 0.810 across the 24 Instruction Induction tasks versus 0.749 for human-engineered prompts (Figure 1b), and achieves zero-shot accuracy at or above the human bar on all 24 of 24 individual tasks while the Greedy baseline trails on most (Figure 4). On the BIG-Bench Instruction Induction subset, APE matches or beats humans on 17 of 21 curated tasks. On TruthfulQA, APE-generated prompts steer the model toward truthful or informative outputs on demand, beating the human “help” prompt with 200 candidate proposals. Prepending APE prompts to few-shot in-context learning prompts also improves downstream performance on 21 of 24 tasks.

My Notes

  • A benchmark designed to favor short prompts. The 24-of-24 headline comes from Instruction Induction [2] tasks (singularize, translate, capitalize, etc.), which are short, template-shaped tasks where human prompt writers have little advantage. A crisp one-sentence instruction is close to the Bayes-optimal prompt, and LLMs can generate dozens of paraphrases of “output the plural form” cheaply. The result does not transfer to tasks where the useful prompt is paragraphs long, contains domain-specific scaffolding, or requires carefully chosen few-shot demonstrations. Later optimizers like MIPROv2 [4] and GEPA [5] target that harder regime.
  • Reverse infilling, the transferable idea. Forward generation (“here are examples, write the instruction”) forces the instruction to be predicted at the end of the prompt, which is rarely where instructions naturally sit. The reverse infilling prompt, which feeds inputs on the left and outputs on the right and asks the model to fill in the instruction between them, lets the instruction be placed mid-prompt where it more naturally belongs. This matches what T5-style span corruption [6] showed about bidirectional objectives years earlier, and it sits in the same family as the prompt-repetition trick for recovering bidirectional context inside a causal LM. Both are runtime workarounds for the fact that left-to-right generation can’t condition on what comes after the token being predicted.
  • Scoring dominates the compute budget. APE’s compute is spent evaluating candidates on a held-out set with the executor LLM, not generating candidates with the proposer. The Monte Carlo resampling step, the only part of APE that resembles iterative optimization, does not add much over the base proposer pool for most tasks. The subsequent line of work (MIPROv2 [4] Bayesian surrogate, GEPA [5] reflective mutation, Promptbreeder [7] evolutionary operators) all attack this scoring bottleneck with different mechanisms.
  • The thin human baseline. The “human” prompts in the benchmark are typically one-sentence instructions written by a small number of annotators under Honovich et al.’s protocol [2], not prompts tuned by expert prompt engineers with access to the executor’s failure modes. The paper’s headline claim is more accurately read as “APE matches a single-shot human annotator on short template tasks.” The gap to genuine prompt-engineering expertise on open-ended tasks is a separate question the paper does not answer.

item.title: GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning [1] (ICLR 2026 Oral), Lakshya A. Agrawal (UC Berkeley), Matei Zaharia (UC Berkeley / Databricks), Omar Khattab (MIT), and 14 co-authors across UC Berkeley, Stanford, Notre Dame, BespokeLabs.ai, Databricks, and MIT argue that natural-language reflection on sampled trajectories is a richer learning signal than scalar rewards, and introduce GEPA (Genetic-Pareto), a prompt optimizer that outperforms Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [2] while using far fewer rollouts.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly adapted to downstream tasks via reinforcement learning (RL) methods like Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), which often require thousands of rollouts to learn new tasks. We argue that the interpretable nature of language often provides a much richer learning medium for LLMs, compared to policy gradients derived from sparse, scalar rewards. To test this, we introduce GEPA (Genetic-Pareto), a prompt optimizer that thoroughly incorporates natural language reflection to learn high-level rules from trial and error. Given any AI system containing one or more LLM prompts, GEPA samples trajectories (e.g., reasoning, tool calls, and tool outputs) and reflects on them in natural language to diagnose problems, propose and test prompt updates, and combine complementary lessons from the Pareto frontier of its own attempts. As a result of GEPA’s design, it can often turn even just a few rollouts into a large quality gain. Across six tasks, GEPA outperforms GRPO by 6% on average and by up to 20%, while using up to 35x fewer rollouts. GEPA also outperforms the leading prompt optimizer, MIPROv2, by over 10% (e.g., +12% accuracy on AIME-2025), and demonstrates promising results as an inference-time search strategy for code optimization. We release our code at https://github.com/gepa-ai/gepa.

Methods

A compound AI system, in the paper’s (and DSPy’s) vocabulary, is a pipeline of one or more LLM-invoked modules — each a distinct prompted call (e.g., a first-hop query generator, a second-hop query generator, an answer generator in a multi-hop QA pipeline) — potentially interleaved with tool calls. Each module has its own prompt, which GEPA can optimize independently.

GEPA treats each prompt in a compound AI system as a gene and maintains a pool of candidate programs. At each iteration (Figure 3), GEPA proposes a new candidate using one of two genetic operators — a single-parent mutation or a two-parent crossover — and evaluates it on a minibatch. If the minibatch score improves over the parent, the candidate is promoted to evaluation on the full training set and added to the pool. The default operator is reflective mutation; crossover (Merge) fires opportunistically when the pool contains two candidates that share a common ancestor, have optimized disjoint sets of prompts, are both Pareto-optimal, and both beat the ancestor in aggregate — with a hard cap of five merges per run.

The two operators are:

  • Reflective Prompt Mutation samples trajectories from one candidate — reasoning, tool calls, and tool outputs — and feeds them to a reflector LM that writes a natural-language diagnosis of what went wrong and proposes an edited prompt for a single module. Figure 5 traces this on PUPA [3] — a benchmark for privacy-conscious delegation, where a trusted local model must answer user queries containing personally identifiable information (PII) using an untrusted API model as a helper, without leaking PII. Starting from a short base instruction (“Create a privacy-preserving request for a powerful external LLM that can assist without learning private information about the user.”), each successful child adds a concrete nuance the reflector extracted from a failure — expanded privacy strategies, explicit PII categories and generalizations, structured output and domain best-practices, then a detailed transformation rationale, ending at a strict exhaustive protocol that bans partial redaction and demands auditable zero-leakage. The prompt accumulates lessons rather than being rewritten wholesale. In the figure below, red arrows mark the promoted lineage from candidate 0 to the best candidate (11), with scores in parentheses.
  • System-Aware Merge takes two qualifying descendants of a common ancestor and assembles a child module-by-module. For each module, if one descendant changed the ancestor’s prompt and the other left it untouched, the child inherits the changed version; if both descendants changed it, the child inherits from the higher-scoring parent (ties broken randomly); if neither changed it, it stays at the ancestor’s version. No LLM call is made — the whole step is a textual combine over existing prompts, which is why the paper calls it system-aware crossover rather than a mutation. Merge works only when the two parents have explored disjoint modules, so complementary improvements can compose without stepping on each other.

Parent selection is Pareto-based rather than greedy. Instead of always mutating the best-scoring candidate, GEPA maintains a per-task score matrix over its history and samples parents from the Pareto frontier — the set of candidates that no other candidate beats on every task — which prevents a locally strong candidate from dominating the search. The paper reports two named variants, “GEPA” using reflective mutation only and “GEPA+Merge” using both mutation and merge; both share the Pareto-based selector and the minibatch-then-full-set gate. The optimizer is agnostic to the downstream task: it needs a trajectory sampler, a metric, and a reflector LM.

Results

Six tasks — HotpotQA [4], HoVer [5], IFBench [6], PUPA [3], AIME-2025 [7], and LiveBench-Math [8] — using GPT-4.1 Mini and Qwen3-8B as task models.

  • Qwen3-8B: GEPA beats GRPO on five of the six benchmarks, losing only on AIME-2025. IFBench makes the gap sharp — GEPA reaches 38.61% after 678 rollouts, above GRPO’s 35.88% at 24,000. Averaged across the six tasks, GEPA is +6% over GRPO and up to +20% on the best task, with up to fewer rollouts (trajectories sampled from the current policy during training). GEPA+Merge is less reliable here: it also trails GRPO on IFBench and PUPA, which the paper attributes to Merge’s hyperparameters being tuned for GPT-4.1 Mini rather than Qwen3-8B.
  • GPT-4.1 Mini: GEPA is evaluated as a drop-in prompt optimizer against MIPROv2 [9] in two settings (instruction-only “MIPROv2-No-Demos” and joint instruction-plus-few-shot “MIPROv2”), Trace [10] with its OptoPrime optimizer, and TextGrad [11] . GEPA wins on every benchmark, with margins as wide as 11% (HotpotQA, PUPA). The abstract highlights +12% on AIME-2025. A GEPA-Qwen-Opt variant optimized entirely on Qwen3-8B gets +9% when run on GPT-4.1 Mini without modification, outperforming every baseline that was optimized directly on GPT-4.1 Mini.

Beyond benchmarks, the paper reports GEPA as a promising inference-time search strategy for CUDA kernel optimization, iteratively improving kernels against a PyTorch-eager baseline.

My Notes

  • Reflection beats policy gradients: GRPO wastes signal already present in each trajectory, in three ways.
    • Information content: GRPO consumes a trajectory as a single scalar reward (normalized against the group’s own mean and standard deviation, the “Group Relative” that replaces PPO’s learned critic), throwing away which tool call was wrong, which instruction was ambiguous, which demonstration misled the model. A reflector LM reading the same trajectory can name all three and edit the one prompt that caused the failure.
    • Variance: because each rollout contributes one noisy scalar, GRPO needs thousands of rollouts before the gradient estimate stabilizes. A natural-language critique encodes structured per-module diagnosis, so one rollout already yields usable signal.
    • Credit assignment: GRPO’s policy-gradient update spreads the scalar reward across every token of every module in the rollout, even when only one module was responsible. Reflection attributes the failure to a single module and leaves the rest alone.
    • The same pattern shows up in Self-Refine and Reflexion, where verbal feedback outperforms scalar reward at comparable compute. GEPA is the first paper I have seen that posts the head-to-head against GRPO on matched tasks.
  • The Pareto-frontier selector is the generalizable part: Sampling mutation parents from the Pareto frontier rather than argmax prevents collapse to a single best candidate, which is the same mode-collapse problem that shows up in evolutionary prompt search and RL fine-tuning. The mechanism is general enough to drop into any iterative search where candidates have multi-dimensional scores (accuracy vs. cost, or task A vs. task B), and I expect to see it reused well past prompt optimization.
  • Beating MIPROv2 without Bayesian optimization: This is a substantive methodological claim. MIPROv2 [9] spends its budget on a Bayesian surrogate over instruction and demonstration hyperparameters. GEPA discards the surrogate and spends the same budget on reflective rewrites plus merge. The result suggests the Bayesian model in MIPROv2 was under-using the trajectory information MIPROv2 already had access to, and the proposer was not reading the failures carefully enough. Several authors overlap between the two papers, so the comparison is a within-lab course-correction rather than an external critique.
  • The paper doesn’t say what reflector it used: Appendix E.2 lists Qwen3-8B and GPT-4.1 Mini as the task models but never specifies the reflection LM. The gepa-ai/gepa repo quickstart pairs GPT-5 as reflector with GPT-4.1 Mini as task, a stronger model reading a weaker one’s trajectories. Without the reflector spec or an ablation, we can’t tell whether GEPA corroborates or contradicts the just-ask calibration [12] and uncertainty-quantification findings that single-model self-evaluation is unreliable.

item.title: Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning (SCoRe)
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning [1] (ICLR 2025 Oral; arXiv preprint September 2024), Aviral Kumar, Vincent Zhuang, Rishabh Agarwal, Yi Su, and 14 co-authors at Google DeepMind train a single model to revise its own answers using only self-generated data, with no teacher model and no oracle feedback.

Self-correction is a highly desirable capability of large language models (LLMs), yet it has consistently been found to be largely ineffective in modern LLMs. Current methods for training self-correction typically depend on either multiple models, a more advanced model, or additional forms of supervision. To address these shortcomings, we develop a multi-turn online reinforcement learning (RL) approach, SCoRe, that significantly improves an LLM’s self-correction ability using entirely self-generated data. To build SCoRe, we first show that variants of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on offline model-generated correction traces are often insufficient for instilling self-correction behavior. In particular, we observe that training via SFT falls prey to either a distribution mismatch between mistakes made by the data-collection policy and the model’s own responses, or to behavior collapse, where learning implicitly prefers only a certain mode of correction behavior that is often not effective at self-correction on test problems. SCoRe addresses these challenges by training under the model’s own distribution of self-generated correction traces and using appropriate regularization to steer the learning process into learning a self-correction behavior that is effective at test time as opposed to fitting high-reward responses for a given prompt. This regularization process includes an initial phase of multi-turn RL on a base model to generate a policy initialization that is less susceptible to collapse, followed by using a reward bonus to amplify self-correction. With Gemini 1.0 Pro and 1.5 Flash models, we find that SCoRe achieves state-of-the-art self-correction performance, improving the base models’ self-correction by 15.6% and 9.1% respectively on MATH and HumanEval.

Methods

Problem setting

This change in problem setup matters because it changes what the model is incentivized to do. A one-turn model trained to minimize loss on learns to commit to its best guess. A two-turn model trained to minimize loss on is free to produce an exploratory first attempt and use the second turn to fix it, as long as the training signal actually rewards that behavior. That training-signal design is the problem the rest of the paper solves.

Formally, the paper states the training objective as Equation 1:

where is the policy (the LLM) with parameters , is the input prompt drawn with its ground-truth answer from dataset , is the model’s attempt at turn conditioned on all prior attempts and optional external inputs (e.g., an instruction to “try again”), and is the verifier’s correctness reward. The paper sets , giving two turns and rewarding the sum .

Two subtleties: first, unlike single-turn SFT or RLHF — which directly supervise the policy to produce — Equation 1 supervises each turn only indirectly, through its contribution to the sum. Second, summing the per-turn rewards means the idealized objective pays equally for a correct first attempt and a correct second attempt. The paper later argues this is exactly why naive RL on Equation 1 behavior-collapses: the policy finds it easier to maximize the sum by producing the best possible and echoing it as than by learning genuine revision. SCoRe’s Stage I regularization and Stage II progress bonus are then introduced as modifications that break this degenerate solution.

The two-stage recipe

The method is a two-stage multi-turn online Reinforcement Learning (RL) recipe. Figure 7 sketches the overall approach:

Stage I optimizes only the second-turn reward while holding the first-turn policy close to the base model via a strict KL penalty:

Here is a large KL coefficient that applies only to the first attempt, preventing the policy from collapsing the two attempts into a single distribution. The result is an initialization where remains base-model-like — so any gain at must come from real revision — while the revision head has started to learn what useful corrections look like. This blocks the dominant failure mode of naive RL on this task, which the paper calls behavior collapse: the model learns to produce a near-optimal first answer and then make no meaningful second-turn revision.

Stage II then jointly optimizes both turns with standard multi-turn RL, initialized from Stage I:

Equation 4 on its own would still permit behavior collapse: the policy can maximize the sum by producing the best possible and echoing it as . SCoRe prevents this by adding a progress bonus to the second-turn reward:

The bonus is positive only when the second attempt flips an incorrect response to correct, and sharply negative when it corrupts a correct response into an incorrect one. Revisions that make progress get more reward than revisions that preserve an already-correct answer, biasing the policy toward genuine self-correction.

Why SFT baselines fall short

Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on model-generated correction traces is shown to fail for a separate reason: distribution shift between the mistakes in the off-policy data and the mistakes the trained model actually makes at test time.

Results

On MATH [2] with Gemini 1.5 Flash, the base model loses 11.2% at the second turn (intrinsic self-correction is net negative), SFT and STaR [3] are near-zero gain, and SCoRe gains +4.4%. The top-line 15.6-point gain on MATH and 9.1-point gain on HumanEval [4] are reported as improvements in the self-correction delta Δ(t1, t2) relative to the base model’s Δ(t1, t2). At matched inference-sample budgets, sequential self-correction with SCoRe outperforms parallel sampling under self-consistency up to samples.

My Notes

  • The SFT failure here is teacher-forcing exposure bias, one level up. Teacher forcing mismatches at the token level: training feeds the gold previous token as input, inference feeds the model’s own previous token. SCoRe’s offline SFT mismatches at the turn level: training’s “first answer” is a frozen sample from the data-collection policy, inference’s “first answer” comes from an updated model whose error distribution has drifted. Same structural problem one level up. The remedies parallel too. Scheduled sampling [5] and DAgger [6] feed the model’s own predictions back into the training loop. SCoRe uses online multi-turn RL to re-sample traces from the current policy each step. The principle is “put the model’s own distribution inside the training loop,” and any self-correction recipe that stops at offline SFT reproduces the exposure-bias pitfall at a coarser granularity.
  • Behavior collapse is not model collapse [7], but the remedies parallel. Shumailov et al.’s model-collapse result describes how recursive training on model-generated text erodes distribution tails across generations — finite-sample statistical error compounds into irreversible drift. SCoRe’s behavior collapse is a different pathology on a single training run: the policy converges to a degenerate solution where the second attempt echoes the first. Both failure modes arise from training on self-generated data without an external anchor. SCoRe’s defenses (a KL penalty against the base model in both stages, plus a ground-truth verifier reward) play the same structural role as the model-collapse literature’s call to keep real data in the loop: they tether the policy to a distribution the policy itself did not produce. The paper never describes the Stage I KL constraint as collapse insurance, but structurally that is what it is.
  • Sequential vs. parallel scaling is the practical implication. Figure 1 right shows that spending samples on sequential self-correction beats the same budget spent on parallel independent samples under self-consistency. That shifts the usual test-time-compute scaling picture [8]: when the model can reliably fix its own mistakes, sequential samples dominate. Practitioners running agent loops will take this as evidence for investing in multi-turn policies rather than larger parallel fan-outs.
  • No PRMs here. Prior work on Let’s Verify Step by Step [9] and later step-level RL pipelines use process-reward models (PRMs) as a source of dense intra-step feedback. SCoRe instead uses only outcome reward plus a turn-level progress bonus, avoiding PRMs entirely. Whether PRM supervision would stack additively with SCoRe, or overlap with the same failure mode the progress bonus already addresses, remains open. Both mechanisms densify a sparse outcome signal, and the paper does not run the controlled comparison between a PRM-based recipe and SCoRe’s ORM+progress-bonus at matched compute.
